Two years after his initial treatment, he experienced a biochemical recurrence with a rising PSA, at which time androgen deprivation therapy (ADT) with a GnRH agonist was initiated, resulting in castrate levels of testosterone (<20 ng/dL). Over the past year, he developed castration-resistant prostate cancer (CRPC), defined by a rising PSA despite ongoing ADT, but imaging studies including bone scan and CT of the abdomen and pelvis have remained negative for distant metastases. Due to a prostate-specific antigen doubling time (PSADT) of 8 months, the decision was made eight months ago to initiate secondary hormone therapy with a novel androgen receptor inhibitor in addition to continued ADT. Since starting this regimen, his PSA has stabilized without further rise, and repeat imaging continues to show no evidence of metastatic disease. At this visit, he reports no new symptoms, and laboratory tests confirm ongoing castrate testosterone and stable PSA. Given these findings, what is the most appropriate next management step for this patient?
